User Guide

This guide covers everyday use of DoubleFloats: creating values, what accuracy to expect, and how the elementary, special, and matrix functions behave. For how things work internally, see the Technical Guide.

The types

typebuilt fromsignificanddecimal digitsexponent range
Double64two Float64106 bits~32same as Float64
Double32two Float3248 bits~14same as Float32
Double16two Float1622 bits~6same as Float16

ComplexDF64, ComplexDF32, ComplexDF16 are the complex counterparts.

Double64 is the recommended type. It is faster and more precise than Double32/Double16 (which mainly exist for completeness), and much faster than BigFloat at comparable precision in typical workloads. The values are immutable bitstypes, and ordinary scalar arithmetic does not allocate.

Constructing values

using DoubleFloats

Double64(2)          # exact: integers convert exactly
Double64(2) / 10     # 0.2 to full Double64 precision
df64"0.2"            # string literal: 0.2 to full Double64 precision
Double64(0.2)        # NOT 1/5: 0.2 is rounded to Float64 *first*

The last line is the most common pitfall: a decimal literal like 0.2 is already a Float64 approximation before Double64 sees it. Use integer ratios or the string macros (df64"...", df32"...", df16"...") whenever a decimal constant must be exact to full precision.

showtyped, stringtyped, and parse round-trip values exactly:

julia> x = sqrt(Double64(2));
julia> showtyped(x)
Double64(1.4142135623730951, -9.667293313452913e-17)
julia> parse(Double64, stringtyped(x)) === x
true

What accuracy to expect

One unit in the last place (ulp) of Double64 is about 2⁻¹⁰⁴ ≈ 4.9e-32 relative. The elementary functions generally deliver working-precision accuracy. In the Accuracy Report, the sampled maximum error varies by function and input range. For example, the sampled worst case for exp on (-100, 100) is about 3.3 ulps.

Boundary behavior worth knowing:

  • For Double64, exp(x) overflows near x ≈ 709.78 and rounds to zero near x ≈ -745.13. As the result approaches zero its low limb eventually runs out of representable bits. Subnormal results from exp, exp2, and exp10 on Double64 and Double32 round to the nearest value on the underlying float's subnormal grid. For example, exp2(Double64(-1075.0)) rounds to zero, while exp2(Double64(-1075.0, 1e-30)) returns the smallest positive Float64 subnormal as a Double64.
  • A finite positive logarithm argument can have a tiny low limb, even when its high limb is far from zero. Mantissa normalization accounts for low limbs that would become subnormal during scaling.
  • Scalar cbrt returns the same double-word type as its argument. Double64 cube roots retain working precision at extreme magnitudes through scaling before refinement.
  • sinh/cosh stay finite through x ≈ 710.47.
  • Relative accuracy near the zeros of sin/cos is limited by the condition of the function itself; absolute accuracy stays at the 2⁻¹⁰⁴ level.

Elementary and special functions

All the familiar functions are available; see Capabilities for the full list. Special functions include erf, erfc, gamma, loggamma, Bessel functions besselj0/j1/y0/y1, besselj(n, x), bessely(n, x), the arithmetic-geometric mean agm(a, b) / agm1(x), and the complete elliptic integral ellipk(m) (accurate over the whole domain 0 ≤ m < 1, including arbitrarily close to m = 1).

erf, erfc, gamma, and the Bessel functions are computed through Float128 (113-bit) arithmetic, which caps them at roughly half a Double64 ulp — in practice, full accuracy.

Elementwise operations on vectors

Use DoubleFloats.simdmap! to apply a scalar function to preallocated vectors. The call returns the destination. For example, sincos stores one (sin, cos) tuple per element, and ^ can reuse a scalar exponent across the batch.

using DoubleFloats

x = Double64.(range(0.01, 0.08; length=4096))
y = similar(x)
DoubleFloats.simdmap!(sin, y, x)

pairs = Vector{Tuple{Double64,Double64}}(undef, length(x))
DoubleFloats.simdmap!(sincos, pairs, x)

DoubleFloats.simdmap!(^, y, x, 5)
DoubleFloats.simdmap!(atan, y, x, reverse(x))

Every vector must have the same axes as the destination. A mismatch throws DimensionMismatch before any writes. The operation uses elementwise indexing without broadcast expansion. Assignment uses the destination's usual conversion rules. For example, a cis call on a real NaN produces a real NaN, which is then converted if the destination holds complex values. Overlapping inputs, including exact in-place and shifted overlaps, are read from their values at entry. Snapshots can allocate. Custom vector storage also uses snapshots when overlap cannot be ruled out.

By default the operation is serial. If a scalar call or assignment throws, earlier elements have been written and later elements keep their original values. Dense, disjoint Double64 and ComplexDF64 vectors can use SIMD for supported operations and input ranges. Views, other precisions, unsupported result types, and out-of-range inputs use scalar methods.

Pass threaded=true to allow eligible operations to run on multiple Julia threads. Run Julia with multiple threads, for example julia -t 4. Threading requires sufficiently long, disjoint dense vectors and works for many functions that use scalar arithmetic internally. Custom callables still run in index order. If a worker fails, the call can raise a task exception after other chunks have written to the destination. Keep the default when the order of writes on failure matters.

See the Technical Guide for SIMD coverage and measured performance.

Linear algebra

using DoubleFloats, LinearAlgebra

Everything routine works with Double64/ComplexDF64 matrices: lu, qr (plain and pivoted), lq, cholesky, svd, eigen, schur, hessenberg, bunchkaufman, \ (square and least squares), det, inv, pinv, nullspace, rank, cond, opnorm, sylvester, and lyap.

eigen follows the same conventions as the LAPACK route for Float64: symmetric/Hermitian input yields real eigenvalues and orthonormal vectors; a real matrix whose spectrum is entirely real yields a real factorization; eigenvalues are sorted by (real, imag).

Functions of matrices

exp, log, sqrt, and the trigonometric/hyperbolic families work on every square matrix, including defective (non-diagonalizable) ones, using dense Schur-based and scaling-and-squaring algorithms:

julia> exp(Double64[1 1; 0 1])     # defective; diagonalization would fail
2×2 Matrix{Double64}:
 2.71828  2.71828
 0.0      2.71828

Real matrices give real results whenever the mathematical result is real (e.g. exp of any real matrix, sqrt/log of matrices without negative real eigenvalues). A negative real eigenvalue makes sqrt/log genuinely complex, and the result type reflects that.

The remaining families (cbrt, sinpi/cospi, and the inverse trigonometric/hyperbolic functions of matrices) use eigen-diagonalization and require a diagonalizable argument.

Performance

See the Benchmark Report for representative timings. Exponential inputs guaranteed to round to zero skip the polynomial. A subnormal result close enough to a rounding midpoint can require a higher-precision fallback, which takes longer and allocates. Near-cancelling Double64 fma and muladd calls also do more work than ordinary calls, using an allocation-free refinement.
